title: Differential targeting of the nucleosome surface and superhelical crevice sites with Ru and Os organometallic agents.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed all 6 files in the Zenodo deposit via its application programming interface (5.83 GB total: 3.0 GB HIS_site.zip, 1.66 GB OsASN-C_GLU_MIX.zip, 977 MB RAPTA-C_GLU.zip, 124 MB bader_volume.zip, 41 MB visualization zip, 0.45 MB rotational_scan.zip). Downloaded and unpacked rotational_scan.zip (34 files): it holds 2 compounds' geometry files plus energy_results.dat with 7 quantum-chemistry energies each. Unpacked the journal supplement: only figure images, a PDF of supplementary information and one video - no data tables. Confirmed all 6 crystal structures (Protein Data Bank entries 9RY3, 9RXV, 9RXU, 9RYA, 9RZK, 9RZN) return HTTP 200 and download. Read the paper's Table 4, which is the complete binding-result table: 6 compounds x 3 sites.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The interpretation of which binding sites are 'surface patches' versus 'superhelical crevice', the molecular-dynamics and thermodynamic-integration free-energy numbers, and the crystallographic refinement statistics in Tables 1-2. I did not open the three multi-gigabyte trajectory archives (each is far over the 50 MB cap).

a1_downloadable.note: Open: Zenodo deposit under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (checked the metadata), and all six Protein Data Bank entries download without login (I fetched headers for all six, all HTTP 200).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no label column anywhere in the files. The only outcome - which metal adducts form where - exists as Table 4 in the article text (anomalous X-ray difference peak heights in sigma units) and would have to be hand-transcribed from the paper or re-derived from electron-density maps.

a3_inputs_present.note: Compound structures are present as atomic coordinate files (.xyz) for 2 compounds, and the nucleosome structures are full crystallographic coordinate files; nothing needs identifier lookup.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated clearly throughout: anomalous difference peak heights in sigma, energies in Hartree in energy_results.dat, distances in angstroms, concentrations in millimolar.

a5_enough_rows.note: FATAL. The entire measured dataset is 6 ruthenium compounds x 3 binding sites = 18 cells in Table 4, of which 14 are populated, backed by 6 crystal structures. The quantum data is 14 energy points across 2 compounds. The checklist needs about 1,500 labelled rows, or 400 for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 5.83 GB of Zenodo archives (molecular-dynamics trajectories), of which 3.0 GB is a single file
a6_fits_laptop.note: The crystal structures and the small scan file fit easily, but the simulation trajectories - the only bulk data here - exceed the ~5 GB working-set limit and the project's 50 MB per-file download rule. Not independently fatal since the tabular part is tiny, but it means there is no laptop-sized bulk data either.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Six crystal structures claimed in the data availability statement, six Protein Data Bank entries live; six compounds in Table 4 match the six arene ligands described in the methods.

a8_label_provenance.note: The binding-site evidence is a physical measurement - anomalous X-ray scattering from the ruthenium atom in a diffraction experiment - not a model output. Provenance is clean; there simply is not enough of it.

existing_models.name: Metal3D (a three-dimensional convolutional neural network that predicts where metal ions sit in a protein structure, Nature Communications 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved in detail; the published report describes sub-angstrom placement accuracy for zinc on held-out Protein Data Bank structures.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read (search result only); generally, coverage of metals other than zinc.

existing_models.name: PinMyMetal (a hybrid machine-learning system for placing transition metals in macromolecules, Nature Communications 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved; described as tailored to four- and six-coordinate metal geometries.

existing_models.name: ESMBind / PRIME / MetalBind (protein-language-model based residue-level metal-binding predictors, 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved; all are recent and report residue-level metal-binding performance on Protein Data Bank derived splits.

existing_models.name: Predicting unknown binding sites for transition-metal-based compounds in proteins (PMC13249218), a companion computational study linked to this paper's PubMed Central record
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved beyond the title; it is the most directly relevant prior work and already tackles the exact question this data would be used for.

backbone.name: None that fits - ESM-2 (a protein language model) would see only one protein, the nucleosome, which is identical across every row

integration.partner_dataset: MetalPDB / the Protein Data Bank's transition-metal complex entries, joinable on Protein Data Bank identifier
integration.join_key: PDB ID and chemical component identifier
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could not write one that this paper's 6 structures would materially advance - the 18 measurements add a rounding error to resources that already hold tens of thousands of metal sites.

controls.positive_control: In principle, the model should rediscover the known preference of ruthenium arene agents for histone glutamate clusters over DNA - but with 14 populated cells there is nothing to hold out.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is meaningless at n=14.
controls.external_validation: Earlier nucleosome-adduct structures from the same group (e.g. 3MNN, 5DNM) exist, but they are the same lab, same crystal form, same handful of compounds.

honest_claim_h3: With 6 compounds and 14 measured adduct observations in one crystal form from one laboratory, no model trained on this data could claim anything beyond a restatement of the paper's own table.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a metal compound's chemical structure to predict which pocket of the nucleosome it will stick to.
plain_idea.train_on: What the model would see: the atomic structure of a ruthenium or osmium organometallic compound (its metal, its aromatic 'arene' ligand and its other attached groups). Verified number of compounds with measured outcomes: 6.
plain_idea.predict: Which of three nucleosome binding sites the compound occupies (a glutamate surface patch, a mixed site, or the internal superhelical crevice). The truth comes from anomalous X-ray scattering of the metal atom in a crystal diffraction experiment - a measurement, not a prediction.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Medicinal-inorganic chemists designing chromatin-targeting anticancer agents would use a rule for which ligand changes switch a compound between surface and crevice binding. Here, though, the data is far too small to learn such a rule.

more_or_better_data.why: Six compounds and 6 crystal structures, versus the tens of thousands of metal sites in the Protein Data Bank that Metal3D and the 2025 protein-language-model predictors were trained on.

confidence_score.why: No replicate crystallographic occupancies are tabulated and there are at most 2-3 observations per site class, so per-prediction uncertainty cannot be estimated from this data.

models_beatable.why: The nearest competitors are 2023-2025 models with open code and Protein Data Bank wide evaluation; nothing trainable on 14 observations could be compared to them, let alone beat them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails every condition: there is no shared evaluation split, no baseline to run on these 14 points, and the measurement (anomalous peak height in one crystal form) is not the same quantity the existing models predict.

ml_idea: The only machine-learning idea the data supports - predicting nucleosome binding-site class from organometallic ligand structure - has 6 compounds and 14 measured observations. The Zenodo deposit holds molecular-dynamics trajectories and quantum geometry scans for 2 compounds, which is reproducibility material for a simulation paper, not a feature/label table. A viable version of this project would have to assemble metal-adduct sites from across the Protein Data Bank and MetalPDB, at which point this paper contributes 6 of several thousand structures and is not the project's basis.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the entire usable tabular content is Table 4 (18 cells) plus two 7-line energy files, so a feature table is an afternoon of transcription. The 5.83 GB of trajectories were deliberately not downloaded, per the 50 MB cap.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in the paper's binding-results table - Table 4 is 6 compounds by 3 sites, 14 populated. That single count, which takes one minute, kills the project.

verdict_reason: Part A5 fails hard and A2 fails with it: the whole measured dataset is 6 ruthenium compounds across 3 nucleosome binding sites (14 populated cells in a table inside the article text, not in any file), supported by 6 crystal structures. The 5.83 GB Zenodo deposit is molecular-dynamics trajectories and quantum geometry scans for 2 compounds - reproducibility material for a simulation study, with no label column and no rows to model. Excellent chemistry and fully open data; it is simply three orders of magnitude too small for machine learning, and the adjacent task is already served by Metal3D, PinMyMetal and several 2025 protein-language-model metal-site predictors.
